summary: Defines OSPFv2 extensions for Bit Index Explicit Replication, an architecture for multicast forwarding that needs no per-flow state in intermediate routers and no explicit tree-building protocol. The extensions let routers advertise the information BIER needs.

eli5.summary: Instead of each helper remembering who gets a copy of a message, the sender stamps the list of recipients on it, and routers just follow the stamp.

questions: how does ospfv2 advertise bier information
how does ospf advertise bier information
subtitle: How OSPFv2 routers tell each other the information BIER multicast forwarding needs, in MPLS networks.

tldr.problem: BIER forwards multicast without per-flow state in routers, but every router in the BIER domain still has to learn each other router's BIER identity and label ranges. The architecture lets link-state protocols carry that information.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 8444 defines two new sub-TLVs of the OSPFv2 Extended Prefix TLV: a BIER Sub-TLV (type 9) and a BIER MPLS Encapsulation Sub-TLV (type 10). They are flooded in an area-local Extended Prefix Opaque LSA, and area border routers copy them between areas.
tldr.outcome: OSPFv2 can now advertise BIER information for MPLS encapsulation. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has since been updated by RFC 9272.

today: RFC 8444 is a Proposed Standard and has been updated by RFC 9272, so read the two together. It covers only BIER with MPLS encapsulation.

sections.title: Why BIER Needs OSPF
sections.content:
Bit Index Explicit Replication (BIER) is an architecture for multicast forwarding through a "BIER domain" that does not require intermediate routers to keep multicast-related, per-flow state. It also does not require an explicit tree-building protocol.

A multicast packet enters the domain at a Bit-Forwarding Ingress Router (BFIR) and leaves at one or more Bit-Forwarding Egress Routers (BFERs). The BFIR adds a BIER header that contains a BitString, in which each bit stands for exactly one BFER. The set of bits that are set is the set of egress routers that must receive the packet.

The BIER architecture requires participating routers to exchange BIER-related information within a domain, and it permits link-state routing protocols to distribute it. RFC 8444 describes the OSPF side of that, for BIER with MPLS encapsulation as defined in RFC 8296. Other encapsulation types, and using several encapsulation types together, are outside its scope.
sections.eli5: Each message carries a checklist of which receivers need a copy. For the routers to read the checklist correctly, they first have to agree on which box on the list means which receiver. This RFC is how they agree.

sections.title: Advertising BIER Information in OSPF
sections.content:
All BIER information that a Bit-Forwarding Router (BFR) advertises is tied to its BFR-prefix: a routable IP address, unique within the BIER domain, assigned to each BFR as described in RFC 8279.

Because the information must be associated with a prefix, the authors chose the OSPFv2 Extended Prefix Opaque LSA from RFC 7684 to carry it. Inside the OSPFv2 Extended Prefix TLV, the RFC defines a new sub-TLV for BIER, and that sub-TLV can in turn contain a sub-TLV for MPLS encapsulation.
sections.eli5: Every router has one unique address that acts like its name tag. All the BIER details are stuck onto that name tag, so other routers know whose details they are reading.

sections.title: The BIER Sub-TLV
sections.content:
The BIER Sub-TLV is type 9. Its fixed fields are the sub-domain-id, the MT-ID, the 2-octet BFR-id, BAR and IPA, followed by a Reserved field and optional nested sub-TLVs. Several BIER Sub-TLVs may appear in one Extended Prefix TLV.

  • sub-domain-id identifies the BIER sub-domain within the domain.
  • MT-ID is the Multi-Topology ID, defined in RFC 4915, of the topology associated with the sub-domain.
  • BFR-id is the router's BFR-id. If the BFR has no valid BFR-id configured, it is set to 0, which RFC 8279 defines as illegal.
  • BAR is the BIER Algorithm used to compute underlay paths, taken from the registry in RFC 8401.
  • IPA is the IGP Algorithm that can modify, enhance or replace the path calculation defined by BAR.

The RFC then lists rules for bad input. A sub-domain MUST be tied to exactly one OSPF topology, and an advertisement that conflicts with the local configuration MUST be ignored. If a BFR advertises the same sub-domain-id in several BIER Sub-TLVs, it is treated as if it advertised none for that sub-domain. BFRs MUST detect duplicate valid BFR-ids and then act as RFC 8279 describes. A BAR or IPA value that does not match the local configuration MUST be reported as a misconfiguration and the Sub-TLV MUST be ignored. Non-zero BAR or IPA values are outside the scope of this document.
sections.eli5: This is the main entry in the phone book: which group the router belongs to, its personal number, and which route-finding recipe it uses. If two entries clash, routers ignore the confusing ones instead of guessing.

sections.title: The BIER MPLS Encapsulation Sub-TLV
sections.content:
This is a sub-TLV of the BIER Sub-TLV, type 10, with a length of 8 octets. It MAY appear several times inside one BIER Sub-TLV and carries the MPLS-specific details.

  • Max SI is a 1-octet maximum Set Identifier used in the encapsulation for this sub-domain and BitString length.
  • Label is a 3-octet field whose 20 rightmost bits give the first label of a range. The 4 leftmost bits MUST be ignored.
  • BS Len is a 4-bit BitString length, using the values allowed in RFC 8296.

The label range runs from Label to Label + Max SI. Each Set Identifier maps to one label: the first label is for SI=0, the second for SI=1, and so on. A unique range is allocated for each BitString length and sub-domain-id.

Errors are handled by ignoring. A sub-TLV whose maximum label exceeds the 20-bit range, or whose BitString length is not an allowed value, MUST be ignored. If the same BitString length repeats inside one BIER Sub-TLV, the whole BIER Sub-TLV is ignored. Label ranges advertised by one BFR MUST NOT overlap; if they do, all BIER sub-TLVs from that router MUST be ignored.
sections.eli5: BIER on MPLS uses numbered tickets called labels. This entry says which block of tickets a router uses for each list size, so no two blocks from the same router ever overlap.

sections.title: Flooding Scope and Crossing Areas
sections.content:
The Extended Prefix Opaque LSA that carries the BIER Sub-TLV has an area-local flooding scope. To make BIER work across several OSPF areas, the information has to be passed between areas by the Area Border Routers (ABRs).

When an ABR advertises a Type-3 Summary LSA for a prefix into its attached areas, it also originates an area-local Extended Prefix Opaque LSA with the route-type set to inter-area. To decide whether to add a BIER Sub-TLV, the ABR finds its best path to the prefix in the source area and the router that advertised that path. If that router advertised a BIER Sub-TLV for the prefix, the ABR copies the information into the BIER Sub-TLV for each attached area.

In the RFC's example, R1 advertises 192.0.2.1/32 in Area 1 with a BIER Sub-TLV. ABR R2 copies the entire BIER Sub-TLV, including its sub-TLVs, into the LSA it generates for Area 0, and ABR R3 does the same for Area 2.
sections.eli5: A note pinned up in one town stays in that town. So the border officers photocopy the note and pin it up in the next town, and the next, so everyone gets the same note.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says the new sub-TLVs add no new security risks to OSPF, and the existing OSPF security extensions from RFC 2328 and RFC 7684 apply. It assumes BIER and OSPF sit in a single administrative domain. Where attackers might reach the OSPF routing domain, stronger authentication such as RFC 7474 SHOULD be used.

It also argues that the denial-of-service concern discussed in RFC 8279, setting too many bits in a BitString, cannot be triggered through these advertisements. The BFIR decides which bits to set without being influenced by OSPF control messages, and the OSPF data only builds the forwarding tables that map each bit to next hops.

Implementations MUST detect malformed BIER and BIER MPLS Encapsulation Sub-TLVs so that they cannot crash the OSPF router or process. Malformed TLVs SHOULD be counted or logged, and logging SHOULD be rate-limited.
sections.eli5: Tampering with the phone book cannot make the sender stamp extra names on a message, because the sender picks the names itself. Routers must also stay calm when they read a garbled entry, and not keep shouting about it.

sections.title: IANA Allocations
sections.content: IANA allocated two values from the "OSPFv2 Extended Prefix TLV Sub-TLVs" registry defined in RFC 7684: the BIER Sub-TLV is 9 and the BIER MPLS Encapsulation Sub-TLV is 10.
sections.eli5: The official number keeper gave the two new entries their numbers, 9 and 10, so everyone uses the same ones.

fields.name: Length
fields.desc: Variable, depends on the nested sub-TLVs.

fields.name: sub-domain-id
fields.desc: Identifies the BIER sub-domain within the domain.

fields.name: MT-ID
fields.desc: Multi-Topology ID of the topology tied to the sub-domain.

fields.name: BFR-id
fields.desc: The router's BFR-id; 0 if none is configured.

fields.name: BAR
fields.desc: BIER Algorithm used to compute underlay paths.

fields.name: IPA
fields.desc: IGP Algorithm that modifies or replaces the path calculation.

fields.name: Max SI
fields.desc: Maximum Set Identifier used for this sub-domain and BitString length.

fields.name: Label
fields.desc: Rightmost 20 bits are the first label of the range; the 4 leftmost bits are ignored.

fields.name: Reserved
fields.desc: SHOULD be 0 on transmission, MUST be ignored on reception.
